title: How to File Taxes on Kalshi and Polymarket Earnings
summary: While the IRS hasn't issued formal guidance on prediction markets, your earnings are still taxable. However, the tax treatment on that income can vary. Here's exactly what you need to know before you file.
body_markdown:
## Key takeaways


-


You owe taxes on Kalshi and Polymarket earnings, even if you don’t receive a tax form.


-


The tax rules are still unclear. How you report your earnings depends on what you traded. Don’t assume your trades qualify for the lower tax rates available under Section 1256.


-


Losing money doesn’t necessarily mean you owe no taxes. You may not be able to deduct all your losses from your winnings.


-


Using crypto on Polymarket adds another layer. You may need to report gains or losses from using USDC, in addition to your prediction-market trades.


-


Keep your records. Download your trading history, profit-and-loss statements, and tax forms before filing.


-


Get expert guidance before choosing how to report your trades, especially if you had large winnings and losses. A tax pro can help determine which treatment fits your situation and what losses you can deduct.


Prediction markets have emerged as one of the fastest-growing (and most controversial) corners of American "finance". You can now place a contract on who wins the Super Bowl, whether the Fed raises rates, or even whether Jesus Christ returns before 2027. Platforms like Kalshi and Polymarket let Americans bet on almost anything - over $3.3B was wagered on the 2024 U.S. presidential race alone on Polymarket! That's some wild betting.


But here's where things get tricky. What happens to those earnings? The IRS has yet to issue clear guidance, leaving things open to interpretation. Axios reports that[61% of Americans](https://www.axios.com/2026/03/17/kalshi-polymarket-sports-betting) say prediction market trading is "closer to gambling," while only 8% say it's "closer to investing," according to a March 2026 Ipsos poll of 2,363 adults. Meanwhile, the platforms themselves insist they're offering regulated financial contracts, not bets.


What that means for YOU is your earnings could be treated as ordinary income, capital gains... or something else. And that can swing your tax bill. This guide helps break down the different tax treatments and what you should consider for YOUR taxes.


## Are prediction market earnings taxable?


Yes. Profits from prediction markets are generally taxable even if you don't receive a tax form. The hard part is determining how those profits and losses should be classified.


## How are earnings from Kalshi or Polymarket taxed?


Maybe you bet correctly on a Fed rate decision or... made a good call on whether there'd be more tech layoffs this year or what gas prices would be tomorrow.


But as of 2026, the IRS hasn't issued specific guidance establishing one tax treatment for every prediction-market contract. Depending on the platform and contract, taxpayers and tax professionals may consider the earnings as ordinary income, capital gains or gambling.


That distinction matters because different classifications have different rules for:


-


tax rates,


-


how gains and losses are calculated,


-


which tax forms you use,


-


whether losses can offset other income, and


-


whether special rules such as Section 1256 or the wagering-loss limitation apply.


The appropriate treatment should be based on the actual contract, platform, transaction, and applicable tax law.


### 1. Ordinary Income Treatment


This is the most conservative tax treatment that essentially reports your net profits from prediction markets as "Other Income" on Schedule 1, Line 8z of your[Form 1040](https://www.irs.gov/forms-pubs/about-form-1040) , with a label like "Kalshi prediction market earnings" or "Polymarket contract gains."


Your net gains are taxed at your ordinary income tax rate, which could be anywhere from 10% to 37% depending on your tax bracket. For example, if you're in the 24% tax bracket, and net $12,000 in Kalshi profits, you'd owe $2,880 in federal taxes with this approach.


If you have a net loss, you would not be able to deduct it; your taxable gains would just be $0.


This treatment is straightforward and defensible, but high earners pay more taxes than if the income was treated differently.


### 2. Capital Gains Treatment


Some tax professionals argue that prediction market contracts should be treated as capital assets, similar to stocks or options, with gains and losses reported on Schedule D via[Form 8949](https://www.irs.gov/forms-pubs/about-form-8949) . Under this treatment, positions held for more than one year would qualify for long-term[capital gains](https://www.keepertax.com/capital-gains-tax-calculator) rates (0%, 15%, or 20%).


However, most prediction market contracts resolve quickly (days or weeks), meaning the majority of gains would still be taxed as short-term[capital gains](https://www.keepertax.com/capital-gains-tax-calculator) , which are taxed at the same rate as ordinary income anyway.


Additionally, an extra 3.8% Net Investment Income Tax (NIIT) applies to investment income once modified AGI exceeds $200,000 (single), $250,000 (joint), or $125,000 (married filing separately). That extra tax applies to both short-term and long-term gains.


That said, capital asset treatment allows you to offset losses against gains dollar-for-dollar, which can meaningfully reduce your bill if you've had a rough stretch betting. If your losses exceed your gains, individuals can generally deduct up to $3,000 of net capital losses against other income per year ($1,500 if married filing separately), with unused losses carried forward.


### 3. Section 1256 Contract Treatment


This treatment can result in the lowest tax rate, but is high risk. Section 1256 of the Internal Revenue Code covers a specific category of regulated futures contracts. Gains and losses from these contracts are taxed using a 60/40 split: 60% is treated as long-term capital gains (regardless of how long you held the position), and 40% as short-term. That blended rate is significantly lower for most traders.


For example, a trader in the 32% bracket with $50,000 in Kalshi gains would owe roughly $10,900 under Section 1256 treatment versus approximately $16,000 at ordinary income rates!


While all that sounds nice on paper, the problem arises in whether Kalshi event contracts qualify as Section 1256 contracts. Kalshi is CFTC-regulated, which makes it a stronger candidate than Polymarket, but the IRS has consistently taken a narrow view of Section 1256 categories.


Section 1256 was written for traditional futures contracts, and prediction market contracts work differently in ways that likely disqualify them. Similar "yes or no" contracts have been sold on regulated exchanges for years, and tax professionals who've studied them generally concluded they don't qualify.


Therefore, without a formal ruling from the IRS, you're operating in murky waters. If you take this position, most CPAs recommend filing[Form 8275](https://www.irs.gov/forms-pubs/about-form-8275) (a disclosure form) to flag the aggressive stance and reduce potential penalties in an audit. We wouldn't recommend pursuing this strategy without professional guidance. Need help? Chat with a[Keeper CPA](https://landing.keepertax.com/onboarding/situations) !


### 4. Gambling Treatment


There's another possibility that deserves particular attention in 2026: Could some prediction-market transactions be treated as wagering transactions for federal income-tax purposes?


The CFTC regulates prediction markets as derivatives markets, and many event contracts are structured as financial contracts. But financial-market regulation doesn't, by itself, definitively answer how every contract should be characterized under the Internal Revenue Code.


This distinction became much more important in the beginning of 2026.


Under current federal law, the deduction for losses from wagering transactions is generally limited to the **lesser of:**


-


90% of wagering losses, or


-


wagering gains.


Congress may still undo the 90% limit. On September 16, 2026, the House Ways and Means Committee voted 38–5 to advance H.R. 10357, which would restore the full deduction for wagering losses (still capped at winnings) starting with the 2026 tax year. As of October 9, 2026, it hasn't passed the full House or the Senate, so for now the 90% limit is the law.


For casual gamblers, gambling losses are generally claimed as itemized deductions. This means that taxpayers who claim the standard deduction are not allowed to claim any losses at all, and will always be taxed on their total wins.


For those who are able to itemize, below are examples of how this works in three different scenarios: when losses are less than winnings, when losses are the same as winning, and when losses are more than winnings.

## Is Kalshi gambling for tax purposes?


Not officially, but some contracts could be. Kalshi is regulated by the CFTC as a Designated Contract Market and treats its products as financial contracts, not bets. That's why it doesn't issue W-2Gs or withhold tax the way a sportsbook does. But financial regulation doesn't decide how the IRS taxes a contract, and as of October 2026, the IRS hasn't ruled either way.


The answer likely depends on what you traded:


-


**Sports contracts:** These are the closest thing to a bet, and the most likely to be treated as gambling. Several states have challenged Kalshi in court, arguing its sports contracts are illegal sports betting.


-


**Economic and financial contracts:** Contracts on things like Fed rate decisions, inflation, or stock index levels look the most like traditional derivatives. They make the strongest case for investment (capital gains) treatment.


-


**Elections, culture, and other events:** These fall somewhere in between, and there's no clear rule for them yet.


Why it matters: if your trades are treated as gambling, you can deduct losses only if you itemize, and starting in 2026, only 90% of them, capped at your winnings. Under capital gains treatment, losses offset your gains, and up to $3,000 of net losses a year can be deducted against other income.

## How to file Kalshi taxes


Kalshi operates as a CFTC-registered Designated Contract Market (DCM).


### What tax documents does Kalshi send you?


Kalshi issues 1099 documentation for certain transactions (interest, bonuses, and crypto transfers), but none of these forms report your event contract trading profits. You'll need to export your full trade history from your account dashboard and calculate your own cost basis and proceeds.


And since the 1099-MISC threshold rose from $600 to $2,000 starting in 2026, many users won't receive one at all.


Tax form


What it's for


Form 1099-INT


Interest payments


Form 1099-MISC


Certain credits and rewards


Form 1099-B


Certain broker transaction proceeds, including crypto transfers


Form 1099-DA


Certain digital-asset transaction reporting


Profit and Loss (P&L) statement


Summarizes trading activity, which includes fees and rebates and is updated monthly


### How to file (using the ordinary income approach):


1.


Export your complete trade history from Kalshi's platform.


2.


Calculate your net profit (total proceeds minus total amounts paid for contracts).


3.


Report that net figure on Schedule 1, Line 8z of your Form 1040, labeled "Kalshi prediction market earnings."


4.


Pay taxes at your ordinary income rate.


### How to file (using the capital gains approach):


1.


Export your complete trade history from Kalshi's platform.


2.


For each contract you sold or that settled during the year, note the date you bought it, the date it closed, what you paid (including fees), and what you received ($1 per contract if it paid out, $0 if it didn't, or the sale price if you sold early).


3.


Sort them into short-term (held one year or less) and long-term (held more than a year). Most prediction market positions will be short-term.


4.


List the transactions on Form 8949. Since Kalshi doesn't send a 1099-B for these trades, check Box C for short-term and Box F for long-term. If you have a lot of trades, you can just enter totals and attach a statement with the details.


5.


Carry the totals to Schedule D. A net gain is taxed at short-term (ordinary) or long-term capital gains rates. A net loss offsets other capital gains, and up to $3,000 of any remaining loss can be deducted against regular income each year, with the rest carrying forward.

What


Capital treatment

Qualifying contracts have their own gain-and-loss rules, including 60/40 treatment and mark-to-market accounting.

Beginning in 2026, the deductible amount is generally limited to 90% of wagering losses and cannot exceed wagering gains. Losses can only be claimed if the taxpayer itemizes deductions on Schedule A.


## How to file Polymarket taxes


Polymarket launched a U.S.-regulated version in late 2025 through its acquisition of QCEX, a CFTC-licensed exchange. If you're trading on that version, your contracts work much like Kalshi's, and the same tax treatments discussed above apply. Being CFTC-regulated doesn't by itself settle how the IRS will tax them.


### On-chain Polymarket


The on-chain Polymarket product adds another tax issue: **digital assets.** Positions are generally transacted using USDC, a dollar-pegged stablecoin. For U.S. federal tax purposes, the IRS treats digital assets, including stablecoins, as property rather than U.S. currency.


That means on-chain Polymarket activity can potentially create **two separate layers of tax accounting:**


1.


the gain or loss associated with the prediction-market contract, and


2.


gain or loss associated with disposing of USDC or another digital asset.


### How USDC can create a taxable event


Using USDC to purchase property or enter a transaction generally involves disposing of that USDC. If its fair market value when disposed of differs from your tax basis, that can produce a digital-asset gain or loss.


Because USDC is designed to remain close to $1, the economic gain or loss on the stablecoin itself may often be small.


When a contract pays out, you receive USDC. That payout is the result of the contract, not a separate crypto sale. The USDC you receive gets a cost basis equal to its value that day (about $1 per coin), and you'll have a separate, usually tiny, gain or loss on it later when you spend or convert it.


That's why on-chain Polymarket bookkeeping can become complicated quickly.


### What records should Polymarket traders keep?


-


Date of acquisition (when you bought the position)


-


Date of disposition (when you sold or the contract resolved)


-


Proceeds (the USDC value received)


-


Cost basis (what you paid, in USD terms)


-


Resulting gain or loss


For digital assets such as USDC, you may also need:


-


Date of acquisition


-


Tax basis


-


Date of disposition


-


Fair market value at disposition, and


-


Resulting digital-asset gain or loss


[Form 1040](https://www.irs.gov/forms-pubs/about-form-1040) has a checkbox asking whether you received, sold, or exchanged any digital assets. If you traded on Polymarket, the answer is yes. The IRS uses blockchain analytics tools that can trace wallet activity back to individuals through centralized on-ramps and off-ramps (like Coinbase or Kraken, where you converted dollars to crypto).


If you're an active trader with lots of transactions, tools like Koinly, CoinTracker, or specialized services like PolyTax can import your Polygon wallet history, calculate your gains and losses per trade, and generate a pre-filled Form 8949 if you're reporting under the capital gains approach.


## Your next steps: a rough guide


-


**If you traded on Kalshi:** Download your P&L statement, complete transaction history, and tax forms available in your account. Determine the appropriate tax characterization before deciding where the activity belongs on your return. Need help? Book a call with a[Keeper tax pro](https://landing.keepertax.com/onboarding/situations) today.


-


**If you used on-chain Polymarket:** Download your wallet history and preserve your USDC basis and disposition records in addition to your prediction-market records.


-


**If you traded through Polymarket US:** Confirm which entity and contracts you actually traded.


-


**If you had substantial wins and losses:** Get professional guidance. Loss treatment can differ dramatically depending on whether the transactions are characterized as capital assets, qualifying Section 1256 contracts, wagering transactions, or something else.


-


**If you traded on multiple platforms:** Don't assume every contract necessarily receives the same tax treatment.


## FAQs


###

###


Losses may be deductible, depending on how you report them. Under capital gains treatment, losses offset other capital gains, and up to $3,000 of net losses a year ($1,500 if married filing separately) can be deducted against other income, with the rest carried forward. Under ordinary income treatment, losses only reduce your prediction market gains; a net loss isn't deductible. Gambling treatment is the least favorable: starting in 2026, you can deduct only 90% of your losses, capped at your winnings, and only if you itemize deductions on Schedule A.

Regulated prediction markets like Kalshi structure their products as financial contracts and don't issue W-2Gs, but the IRS hasn't said how they should be taxed. Some contracts, especially sports contracts, could be treated as wagers. That's why we lay out four possible tax treatments above.

You still owe tax on those profits whether or not you receive a 1099, so download your full trade history and calculate your net gains yourself.
